findings.title: The "numpy" backend actually measures Numba forces, and Numba is not "a backend that doesn't exist"
findings.description:
The design says NumPy is "the only backend that exists today" (L25-26) and that Numba is out of scope (L92). But slice 118 is complete (`100-slices.behavior-engine.md:61` is `[x]`), and `src/migratory/engine/_jit_config.py:14` sets `USE_JIT_KERNELS: bool = True`. Every `BulkForce.__call__` checks that flag (`flocking.py:82,192,326`, `herding.py:32,175`) and goes to `forces_jit` kernels. The design's NumPy runner "calls `tick()` directly" (L131-132) and never touches the flag. So every `numpy` row, every NumPy parity hash, and the "golden" reference for slices 142/145 would actually be Numba numbers. Slice 142 is defined as Quadrants vs. Numba **and** NumPy (plan L30), so its comparison would be wrong from the start.

The flag is also a module-level global. Running `numpy` and a future `numba` backend in one process (`--all-backends`, L481) means toggling global state, and the design never addresses that. The design must:
- have the `numpy` backend pin `USE_JIT_KERNELS=False` (and restore it in `finalize`), or rename the backend to what it actually measures;
- register a `numba` backend now (one more file). Plan L26 says Numba "slots in as those backends become available", and it is available now.

findings.title: The per-force breakdown the plan assigns to 141 is deferred, and the deferral breaks the "zero harness changes" promise
findings.description:
Plan L26 gives 141 the job of producing timings broken down by phase, including "force totals per force". The design reports one `force_total` and pushes per-force timing to slice 142 by "extending `PhaseTimings` with an optional `force_breakdown`". That extension changes `runner.py` (the dataclass and `_PHASE_FIELDS`), both report renderers, and the JSON `schema_version` (L530-532). This contradicts the Integration Requirement that slice 142 lands with "one file … and zero changes elsewhere in the harness" (L586-588).

Per-force bracketing in `tick_instrumented` is one `perf_counter_ns` pair inside the existing force loop (`tick.py:110-111`). Deliver it in this slice.

findings.title: Numba backend is attributed to slice 144, which is Quadrants Force Kernels
findings.description: L92, L341 and L589-591 say "Slice 144 registers `numba`". Per plan L34, slice 144 ports forces *to Quadrants*. Numba is slice 118, which is already done. The Integration Requirement at L589 names a consumer that won't do that work.

findings.title: The workload schema example is 3D, but the engine is 2D
findings.description: The example has `world_size: [200.0, 200.0, 200.0]` and 3-component `cluster_centers`. `src/migratory/__init__.py:4` sets `DIMS = 2`, and the existing loader rejects anything else (`src/migratory/bench/workload.py:187-191`, "must have 2 entries (DIMS=2)"). The design is the documented schema source (workload.py:8-11), so a workload copied from it fails to load. Fix the example to 2D.

findings.title: Force resolution describes module-level singletons that don't exist, and "five forces" is wrong
findings.description:
L398-399 says force names resolve to "module-level singleton instances … (e.g. `flocking.cohesion_force`)". The engine has no such attributes, only classes (`flocking.py:65,175,311`, `herding.py:14,102,157`). The existing code builds its own instances in `bench/workload.py:67-74`.

L138, L543 and L554 also refer to "the five existing `BulkForce` implementations". There are six: `PropulsionForce` (`herding.py:102`) exists, the server's `force_builder.py:37` includes it, and `config/default.yaml:176` turns it on. The `mid-flock` force list (L379-384) leaves propulsion out but includes leadership and momentum. So it doesn't match the "live-server default" it claims to approximate (L353-355), and it doesn't match the architecture's reference of "4 forces" either (arch L55), which walkthrough step 9 compares against.

findings.title: Profile registry invents profiles the design says it won't invent, and leadership is never populated
findings.description:
L392-395 says `flocker`/`leader` map to "existing `BehavioralProfile` constructors used in `config/default.yaml`" and that "the harness does not invent new profiles". `config/default.yaml:145-182` defines only one profile, `"default"`, with no `max_neighbors`. The existing registry (`bench/workload.py:33-60`) invents a `leader` and adds `max_neighbors=32` to `flocker`. That flips `tick()` onto the kNN fast path (`tick.py:72-84`), which is a different code path from the live default.

Separately, `LeadershipForce` weights neighbours by `state.leadership` (`forces_jit.py:208`). `AgentState.create` sets that array to zero (`state.py:71`), and nothing in the workload schema sets it. So the "leader" profile has no effect, and the leadership force burns time producing zero output (rows with lead_sum < 1e-10 are zeroed, `forces_jit.py:192-193`). The design needs to say where profile values come from (inline in the YAML, or a named file) and how per-agent `leadership` is set.

findings.title: Formation, initial-state and density generation are unspecified, and the plan's `density` input is missing
No bounds handling, so formations drift during 660 ticks
findings.description:
The live sim runs `apply_bounds_policy` after every tick (`migratory_server/simulation.py:11,123`). That lives in `migratory_server.bounds_enforcement`, which the harness is forbidden to import (L145, L573). The workload has a `world_size` but no bounds policy. A `uniform`/`dispersed` start with no walls spreads out freely, and clusters migrate, so the density being measured shifts across 60 warmup and 600 measure ticks. The whole point of the named formation regimes (arch L38, "performance is formation-dependent") is lost.

Fixes: state that bounds are deliberately left out and keep runs short enough that this doesn't matter; or move the policy into the engine (a dependency direction change that needs saying); or make the soft-bounds `WorldBoundsRepulsor` force (`engine/repulsor.py:40`) a workload option.

findings.title: Phase boundaries don't "correspond exactly" to `tick()`, and the risk section puts setup cost in the wrong phase
Parity hash timing is contradictory, and a hash can't support slice 145's tolerance-based parity
findings.description:
The hash is taken "post-warmup" in one place (L81) and "after the measure phase" in another (L460). L471-473 says GPU backends' hashes get interpreted "within the documented tolerance band", and L533-534 says slice 145's parity test uses the NumPy hash as its reference. A SHA-256 only supports exact equality, so no tolerance can be applied to it. Plan L36 defines 145's parity as "within a documented tolerance for non-deterministic GPU reductions". It's also the same trajectory-comparison job the design hands to `tools/run_deterministic_trajectory.py` in Open Questions (L748-755).

Either drop the claim that 145 consumes the hash, or save the final arrays (`.npy`) next to the hash so a tolerance comparison is possible.

findings.title: Registry discovery is unspecified, so "one file, zero changes elsewhere" can't hold
findings.description: `@register_backend` only runs when its module is imported. Nothing says who imports `backends/numpy_backend.py`. If `backends/__init__.py` imports it explicitly, each new backend needs an edit there, which breaks L586-591. If backends are auto-discovered (for example with `pkgutil.iter_modules`), the design has to say so. It also has to say how a Quadrants backend whose package isn't installed is handled at discovery time (skip with a warning, or fail), because L93-95 says 141 doesn't require Quadrants. There's also an API mismatch: Scope L84 describes `register_backend(name, factory)`, while L305 is a decorator that takes only `name`, and the Protocol's `name: str` attribute (L327) duplicates the registry key with no rule for keeping them consistent.

findings.title: The spatial backend is fixed to KDTreeQuery, but slice 143 needs it as a variable
findings.description: Plan L32 says slice 143's `QuadrantsSpatialQuery` is "validated by the harness … timing comparison" against `KDTreeQuery`. In this design the spatial choice is buried inside the backend runner, and the workload has no spatial field. So comparing spatial backends with the same force backend means another backend class for every pairing. The live default is `"adaptive"` (`migratory_server/config.py:293`), not kdtree, which undercuts "current default operating point" (L75, L179). L542 also gives the wrong path, `engine.spatial.KDTreeQuery`. The real one is `migratory.spatial.kd_tree.KDTreeQuery`, and `migratory/spatial/__init__.py` exports nothing.

findings.title: Result-file I/O failure modes are missing
CLI and Markdown aggregation are underspecified, and the walkthrough uses flags the CLI section doesn't define
findings.description: Walkthrough steps 1-2 (L605, L611) use `--list-backends` and `--list-workloads`, which don't appear in the CLI section. Nothing says how `--workload mid-flock` maps to a path. The Markdown report is "one table per workload across all backends in `bench/results/`" (L440), but the directory will hold many runs per backend, across SHAs and platforms, and the design never says which one becomes the row. The `bench/results/*.md` filename is also never given. "Sortable on TPS" (L80) means nothing for a static Markdown table.

findings.title: `tps_observed` and `wall_seconds` are undefined, and the example contradicts itself
findings.description: Plan L26 wants output that "per-tier validation can be automated" against, which means checking TPS. The design never defines `tps_observed`: measure ticks over loop wall time, or 1e9 over mean `total_ns`? The example gives mean `total_ns` = 9.55 ms (about 105 TPS, and 600 ticks would take about 5.7 s), alongside `wall_seconds` 9.21 and `tps_observed` 65.1. Those numbers can't all hold unless there are about 6 ms of unexplained work per tick outside `tick_once`.

findings.title: Proportionality: cut features nothing uses yet
"All new code lives under src/migratory/bench/ and bench/workloads/" contradicts the tests and .gitignore
findings.description: New tests live in `tests/bench/` (`test_runner.py`, `test_workload.py` already exist), and `.gitignore:172-174` is modified. `bench/results/.gitkeep` is also checked in. Reword the requirement to list these paths.

findings.title: Dependency direction and engine/server boundary
findings.description: The harness depends on `migratory.engine` and `TickResult` (`engine/tick_result.py:84`) and not on `migratory_server`. It leaves `tick()` alone, which keeps slice 140's contract and the `from_numpy_state` construction benchmark (`tests/test_tick_result.py:76-90`) intact. The `tick()` signature the design relies on (`tick.py:15-22`) matches. `pyyaml` and `pytest-benchmark` are present (`pyproject.toml:14,73`). `tools/run_deterministic_trajectory.py` exists. The architecture states no harness NFR, so none needs restating.

findings.title: Deferring CUDA, CI gating and wire-in-the-loop work fits the plan
findings.description: Plan L26 says "standalone against NumPy at first", and the wire is a separate problem (plan L70). Leaving out the CUDA matrix and transport benchmarks is consistent, as long as the harness itself stays OS-portable (see the filename finding above).
